- When sentiment turns negative sharply (especially after a spike), model tends to overcorrect downward — reduce forecast lag and avoid deep overshoots.
- High news volume with rising sentiment often triggers over-optimistic forecasts — dampen early peaks and adjust downward if sentiment stabilizes or reverses.
- If sentiment change shows strong positive momentum followed by a sharp drop, model often fails to anticipate reversal — add a mean-reversion buffer to prevent premature peak.
- In low-news periods with stable sentiment, model tends to overestimate mean price — apply a slight downward bias to align with historical mean reversion.
- When sentiment is neutral or mildly negative, model often underestimates downside risk — increase forecast volatility or add a conservative downward offset.
- Model frequently overestimates short-term volatility after spikes — apply smoothing or exponential decay to forecast path for 3–5 days post-spike.
- If sentiment change is consistently negative over 3+ days, model tends to ignore trend — apply a downward bias proportional to sentiment decay rate.
- In high-sentiment periods with low news, model often overestimates upside — reduce forecast by 5–10% if sentiment > 0.7 and news < 1.5.
